dueDate.title: Due date calculator
dueDate.intro: Tap the first day of your last period, or choose conception, IVF transfer or a dating scan, to see your estimated due date and your week on one calendar. Nothing is stored.
dueDate.sentence: Due date around {date}. Most babies arrive between {start} and {end}.
dueDate.metaTitle: Due Date Calculator: Estimate When Your Baby Is Due

faq.q: How is the due date worked out?
faq.a: It is 280 days (40 weeks) after the first day of your last period, moved earlier or later if your cycle is shorter or longer than 28 days. It is an estimate: babies are not all born on their due date, and term runs from 37 to 42 weeks.

faq.q: What if my cycle is longer or shorter than 28 days?
faq.a: Change the cycle length under the calendar. A longer cycle moves the date a little later and a shorter one a little earlier. If your cycles vary a lot, the date is less certain, and your clinician may adjust it.

faq.q: Does the ultrasound date replace this one?
faq.a: If a clinician has given you a due date from a scan, follow theirs. You can also choose "Dating scan" and enter the weeks and days from your report; the calculator takes them as written and does not compare them with your period.

dueDate.methodLabel: How do you know the date?

prompt.transfer: Tap the day of the embryo transfer
prompt.scan: Tap the day of your scan

dueDate.scanNote: This uses the weeks and days on your scan report as written. If your clinician has given you a due date, follow theirs.

ovulation.title: Ovulation and fertile window calculator
ovulation.intro: Tap the first day of your last period and see your likely fertile days on a calendar, as a range, not one day. Free and private.
ovulation.sentence: Likely fertile window {window}. Ovulation around {ovulation}. Next period around {next}.
ovulation.metaTitle: Ovulation Calculator: Your Fertile Days as a Range

faq.q: Why does it show a range, not one day?
faq.a: Ovulation does not fall on the same day of every cycle, and a calendar can only estimate it. So femio shows your likely fertile days as a range, never as one certain date.

faq.q: Can I use it if my cycles are irregular or I have PCOS?
faq.a: You can try it, and it will be honest with you. When your cycles vary too much it says “no confident fertile window this cycle” and explains how to tell afterwards whether you ovulated. With PCOS, ovulation test strips can read positive for much of the cycle, so use them with a second sign and talk to your clinician.

faq.q: What signs can tell me ovulation is near?
faq.a: Many women follow changes in cervical mucus, a positive ovulation test strip (a hormone surge, not proof that you ovulated) and their waking temperature, which can show afterwards that ovulation probably happened but cannot predict it. These signs work best alongside the calendar estimate.

gestationalAge.title: How many weeks pregnant am I?
gestationalAge.intro: Find your pregnancy week and trimester from your last period or due date, shown on a calendar. Free, private, no sign-up.
gestationalAge.metaTitle: How Far Along Am I? Pregnancy Week Calculator

faq.q: Why are weeks counted from my last period?
faq.a: Most women know the first day of their last period and few know the day of conception. So pregnancy is counted from that date, and a full pregnancy is 280 days, or 40 weeks.

faq.q: How do pregnancy weeks turn into months?
faq.a: Months differ in length, so clinicians count in weeks. As a rough guide, 40 weeks is a little over nine months. The calculator shows your week and day and your trimester.

faq.q: Which trimester am I in?
faq.a: The first trimester runs until 14 weeks, the second from 14 to 28 weeks, and the third from 28 weeks until birth. The calculator shows yours for the date you choose.

bmi.title: BMI calculator
bmi.intro: Work out your BMI and what it does and does not tell you before pregnancy. A screening number, not a verdict. Free and private.
bmi.note: BMI is a general screen with limits — it doesn't reflect muscle, build, or body composition. Discuss what's healthy for you with your clinician.
bmi.metaTitle: BMI Calculator for Women Planning Pregnancy

faq.q: What does BMI tell me, and what does it miss?
faq.a: BMI compares your weight with your height. It does not measure fat, muscle or fitness, and on its own it cannot tell you how healthy you are. Use it as a number to discuss with your clinician, not a verdict.

faq.q: Can weight affect getting pregnant?
faq.a: Weight is one of many things a clinician may talk about when you plan a pregnancy, along with your cycles, age and health history. BMI on its own cannot tell you your chances.

faq.q: Is BMI used during pregnancy?
faq.a: This calculator is for before pregnancy. Your weight is expected to change during pregnancy, so do not use this number to judge it; your maternity team follows your weight in their own way.

cycleLength.title: How long is my cycle?
cycleLength.intro: Count your average cycle length from your last periods and see how much it varies. A first step before talking to your doctor.
cycleLength.prompt: Tap the first day of each period you remember
cycleLength.varies: Cycles that vary a lot are common and have many causes. If this is usual for you, mention it to a clinician.
cycleLength.metaTitle: Cycle Length Calculator: Is My Cycle Regular?

faq.q: What cycle length is typical?
faq.a: A cycle runs from the first day of one period to the day before the next. Lengths differ from woman to woman, and your own pattern matters more than any average. femio gives a fertile window for cycles of 21 to 35 days and says “no confident window” outside that range.

faq.q: How do I count my cycle length?
faq.a: Count from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. In the calculator, tap the first day of several recent periods, and it works out your average and how much your cycles vary.

faq.q: When should irregular cycles be checked by a doctor?
faq.a: If your shortest and longest cycles are far apart, femio calls your cycles irregular. If you go about three months without a period, or you are trying to conceive and your cycles are irregular, it is reasonable to talk to a clinician now rather than wait.

period.title: When is my next period due?
period.intro: See when your next period may start, shown as a range from your own cycle length. Works for irregular cycles too. No sign-up.
period.varyNote: Cycles normally vary by a few days. Enter your shortest and longest to see an honest range.
period.resultNote: Each range widens a little further ahead, because each cycle can vary.
period.metaTitle: Period Calculator: When Is My Next Period Due?

faq.q: How is my next period estimated?
faq.a: femio starts from the first day of your last period and adds your cycle length. Because cycles shift, it shows a window that reflects how much your own cycles vary, not one date.

faq.q: Is a period a few days late normal?
faq.a: Cycles shift by a few days for many ordinary reasons, which is why you see a range and no “late” counter. If your period has not come and you could be pregnant, a test is the first step. If about three months pass with no period, talk to a clinician.

faq.q: What if my cycle changes every month?
faq.a: Choose “Irregular / not sure” and enter your shortest and longest cycles, and the window widens to match. If your cycles vary too much, femio says there is no confident window rather than guessing. If your cycles are often irregular, it is reasonable to mention it to a clinician.

pregnancyTest.title: When should I take a pregnancy test?
pregnancyTest.intro: Find the earliest day a home pregnancy test is likely to give a clear result, based on your cycle. Free, private, instant.
pregnancyTest.notePeriod: Most home tests work from the first day of a missed period. Testing earlier can give a negative result even if you are pregnant.
pregnancyTest.noteSex: If you do not know when your period is due, test at least 21 days after you last had unprotected sex.
pregnancyTest.source: Source: NHS, Doing a pregnancy test.
pregnancyTest.sentence: A home pregnancy test is most reliable from {date}.
pregnancyTest.promptSex: Tap the day you last had unprotected sex
pregnancyTest.metaTitle: Pregnancy Test Calculator: When to Test

faq.q: How soon can a home test show a positive?
faq.a: Most home tests work from the first day of a missed period. Testing earlier can give a negative result even if you are pregnant. If you do not know when your period is due, the calculator counts at least 21 days after unprotected sex.

faq.q: Is first-morning urine better?
faq.a: Follow the instructions in your test's box, because brands differ. When you test matters more than the time of day: from the first day of a missed period.

faq.q: My test is negative but my period has not come: what next?
faq.a: A negative test around the first day of a missed period can still be wrong. Test again later, and see a clinician if your period still has not come or if you are worried.

rules.stripLine: An ovulation test strip shows a hormone surge, not proof that you ovulated. A rise in your waking temperature afterwards is a better sign.

rules.redFlag: Seek care now if you have a severe headache, changes in your vision, dizziness or fainting, a fever of 38°C or higher, swelling of the face or hands, difficulty breathing, chest pain or a fast-beating heart, severe nausea and vomiting, pain in the upper abdomen or severe belly pain that doesn't go away, vaginal bleeding or fluid leaking, swelling, redness or pain in a leg or arm, overwhelming tiredness, thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, or if your baby's movements have slowed down, stopped or changed. Contact your maternity unit or local emergency services. If you cannot reach them, go to the nearest emergency department.

handoff.body: It stays on your phone, learns your real cycle as you log, and your records are never uploaded. Android only for now.

pregnancyCalendar.title: Pregnancy calendar, week by week
pregnancyCalendar.intro: Tap your due date or the first day of your last period to see the dates of every pregnancy week, the trimesters, and each week's guide. Nothing is stored.
pregnancyCalendar.metaTitle: Pregnancy Calendar: Your Pregnancy Week by Week, with Dates
pregnancyCalendar.headline: Due date around {date}
pregnancyCalendar.trimesterLine: Second trimester from {second}; third trimester from {third}.
pregnancyCalendar.noGuide: No separate guide for this week

faq.q: How are pregnancy weeks counted?
faq.a: From the first day of your last period, which is 280 days (40 weeks) before the due date. "24 weeks" means 24 completed weeks: from 24 weeks and 0 days to 24 weeks and 6 days.

faq.q: When do the trimesters change?
faq.a: The second trimester starts at 14 weeks and the third at 28 weeks. The calendar shows the date each one starts for your due date.

faq.q: My scan gave a different date. Which should I use?
faq.a: Use the due date your clinician gives you. Choose "Due date" and tap it, and every week follows that date.

weightGain.title: Pregnancy weight gain calculator
weightGain.intro: Enter your weight before pregnancy and your height to see the reference range for total weight gain over the pregnancy, from the Institute of Medicine (2009). Nothing is stored.
weightGain.metaTitle: Pregnancy Weight Gain Calculator: IOM Range by BMI
weightGain.eyebrow: Reference range for total gain over the whole pregnancy
weightGain.noRangeTwinsUnderweight: The Institute of Medicine gives no range for twins when BMI before pregnancy is under 18.5. Your clinician will advise.
weightGain.noRangeMultiples: The Institute of Medicine gives no range for three or more babies. Your clinician will advise.
weightGain.note: This is a reference range for your BMI band before pregnancy, not a target or a judgement. Your clinician may suggest a different range for you.
weightGain.source: Source: Institute of Medicine (2009), "Weight Gain During Pregnancy"; the same ranges are used by CDC and ACOG.
weightGain.outOfRange: Enter a weight from {minW} to {maxW} kg and a height from {minH} to {maxH} cm.

faq.q: How is the range chosen?
faq.a: It depends on your BMI before pregnancy, using the ranges the US Institute of Medicine published in 2009. CDC and ACOG use the same ranges.

faq.q: What if I am expecting twins?
faq.a: The Institute of Medicine gives provisional ranges for twins when BMI before pregnancy was 18.5 or more. For a lower BMI, or for three or more babies, it gives no range, and your clinician will advise.

faq.q: Can my clinician suggest a different range?
faq.a: Yes. These are reference ranges for groups of women. Your clinician knows your health and may suggest a different range for you.

contractionTimer.title: Contraction timer
contractionTimer.intro: Press start when a contraction begins and stop when it eases. You get each one's length and the time between them, ready to read out when you call.
contractionTimer.metaTitle: Contraction Timer: Time Contractions Free, No Sign-up
contractionTimer.sessionNote: Nothing is saved: closing or refreshing this page clears the times.

faq.q: What does the timer measure?
faq.a: How long each contraction lasts, and the time from the start of one to the start of the next, with averages over your last five.

faq.q: Does it tell me when to go to hospital?
faq.a: No. It shows your times so you can read them to your maternity unit, who will tell you what to do. Call whenever you are worried; you do not need to reach a certain number first.

faq.q: Are my times saved?
faq.a: No. They stay on this page only while it is open. The femio app keeps them on your phone.

teenBody.body: Puberty in the order it usually happens, with wide ranges — because there is no single normal.

teenReadiness.body: What to carry, where to keep it, and who to tell. A plan means it is never a surprise.

window.why: Cycles jump around a lot in the first few years, so this is a range rather than a date.
window.passed: That window has passed. It happens, and on its own it isn’t a sign of anything. Log your period when it starts and the next estimate gets better.
window.needData: Log a couple of periods first
window.needDataNote: femio needs two start dates before it can work out a range for you.

reassurance.heading: You’re normal
reassurance.body: In the first year or two, a cycle that is short one month and long the next — or a month with none at all — is what usually happens. It settles on its own.

worthMentioning.heading: Worth saying out loud
worthMentioning.body: Some people find it helps to mention any of these to a parent, another adult they trust, or a doctor: about three months with no period, bleeding that soaks a pad or tampon more often than every one to two hours, or pain that keeps you off school. None of them means something is wrong. They are just worth saying out loud.

privacy.body: Nothing about your health ever reaches an advertiser, and nobody else can read what you log. You can export or delete all of it yourself.

reading.heading: Read about any of it
reading.body: The guides written for your age are still being made. Everything else in the library is here already, and none of it is off-limits to you.

followup.heading: Follow-up after your pregnancy
followup.body: You told us about a condition during pregnancy. These checks are the ones guidance describes afterwards, and they are the ones most often missed — usually because nobody offers them.
followup.glucose: A glucose test, usually offered between about four and twelve weeks after birth
followup.bloodPressure: A blood-pressure review in the first days and again around a week to ten days
followup.overdue: The usual window has passed — worth chasing
followup.note: femio records no result and reads none. Your clinician decides what any of these mean.

moodSupport.heading: How you feel is not a verdict on you
moodSupport.body: Low mood, anxiety and numbness after birth are common and they respond to support. Feeling this way is not a failure and it is not permanent.
moodSupport.cta: What to look for, and who to tell

intrusiveThoughts.heading: Frightening thoughts are more common than anyone says
intrusiveThoughts.body: Sudden, unwanted thoughts about harm coming to your baby happen to most new parents. They are frightening precisely because they are the opposite of what you want, and having them says nothing about what you would do. Telling a clinician about them is safe.
intrusiveThoughts.urgent: If you feel pulled to act on a thought, or unable to stay safe, get help today.

checkIn.heading: How are you doing today?
checkIn.note: There is no right answer and nothing to score. Log what you feel, when you feel like it.

loss.heading: However you feel today is okay.
loss.note: Nothing here celebrates on your behalf, and nothing counts anything. femio keeps your record for as long as you want it.

redFlags.heading: Signs to get checked now
redFlags.body: Heavy bleeding that soaks a pad in an hour · a severe headache that will not go away or changes in your vision · trouble breathing or chest pain · a fever · a red, painful or swollen leg · thoughts of harming yourself or your baby. Contact your maternity team or the emergency services available where you are. The weeks after birth carry real risks, and being seen early is never an overreaction.

about.title: About femio
about.intro: femio is a private companion for trying to conceive and pregnancy: calculators and cited guides on the web, and an Android app that keeps your records on your phone.

points.heading: Our mission
points.body: Give every woman referenced, judgment-free health knowledge and honest tracking she can trust — in her language, on her terms.

points.heading: Learning & tracking
points.body: femio helps you understand and track your health. It is a wellness and education tool, not a medical device, and it never replaces your clinician’s care.

points.heading: Cited guides, honest review labels
points.body: Every guide cites its sources. A guide names a clinician only after that clinician has reviewed it; the others say “clinician review pending”.

points.heading: Honest predictions
points.body: We show ranges and a confidence level, never a single false-certain date.

points.heading: Privacy by design
points.body: Your health data is yours — never sold, never shared with advertisers. You can export or delete it anytime.

points.heading: Four languages
points.body: femio is available in English, Arabic, French and Spanish, with right-to-left layout built in.

editorialPolicy.title: Editorial policy
editorialPolicy.intro: Every guide on femio cites its sources and is editorially checked. A guide names its clinician reviewer only after a clinician has reviewed it; the rest say “clinician review pending” until one has.

points.heading: Evidence over opinion
points.body: Every fact traces to a top-tier source such as WHO, CDC, NHS, or ACOG. We never invent statistics or guideline positions; a claim we cannot source is cut.

points.heading: Honest review labels
points.body: A page says “Reviewed by” and names the clinician only when a clinician has reviewed it. Every other page says “Editorially checked · clinician review pending”. A label never changes without a review.

points.heading: At least two sources per page
points.body: Each guide cites at least two independent sources — at least one from a leading medical body — stored and shown so you can check them yourself.

points.heading: Plain language
points.body: English guides are written at about a grade 6–8 reading level; other languages target the same clarity, with any jargon defined on first use.

points.heading: Safety foregrounded
points.body: Guides include a specific when-to-see-a-doctor section, and a clear seek-care-now box wherever a symptom can be an emergency.

points.heading: Independent of advertising
points.body: Medical content is editorially independent. Advertisers never influence what we publish, and ads are never targeted using your health data.

points.heading: Kept current
points.body: Pages show when they were last updated, and reviewed pages show their review date. We aim to re-check every page at least once a year, and sooner when guidance changes.

medicalReview.title: How we review content
medicalReview.intro: Every guide is editorially checked and cites its sources before it is published. A clinician's name appears on a guide only after that clinician has reviewed it; until then the guide says “clinician review pending”.

points.heading: Written, checked, published
points.body: An author writes to our page standard and adds at least two sources, one of them from a leading medical body. Automated checks confirm the structure, the sources and the wording rules before a page is published.

points.heading: Named reviewers, where there is one
points.body: When a clinician has reviewed a guide, their name, credentials and review date appear on that page.

points.heading: The rest say so
points.body: A guide with no named reviewer says “Editorially checked · clinician review pending”. We are adding reviews, and a label changes only when a clinician has actually reviewed that page.

points.heading: Other languages
points.body: Guides are published in English, Arabic, French and Spanish, and the site's screens and tools are in all four languages. A translated guide carries its own review status, never the English guide's.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.intro: How femio handles your information. Your records stay on your phone. The app has no ads and no tracking. Two optional AI features may use the internet, and this page lists every piece of information that ever leaves your phone or reaches us.

summary.title: The short version
items: The femio app keeps your records on your phone only, in a file encrypted with a key held by your phone’s secure hardware. There is no account and no femio server. We cannot see your records, and we cannot get them back for you.

The app has no ads, no analytics of its own and no tracking tools. It uses the internet only for Google’s AI (to download the on-phone model, and for Cloud boost if you agree to it) and for Google Play (installs, updates, ratings and payments). Google’s AI software may send Google technical usage data; femio adds none of your records to it.

Cloud boost is off unless you agree. If you do, a general question you approve, or four broad facts about your health shown to you first, are sent to Google’s cloud AI for femio. The app keeps a dated record of your choice, and you can turn it off at any time.
The website counts visits without cookies and without Google Analytics or Meta. Ads appear only on article and topic pages, and only after you allow them.
femio is for women aged 18 and over. You can see, copy and delete everything the app holds, yourself, inside the app. A file you choose to share or export goes only where you send it.

points.heading: Who we are
points.body: femio is made by {entity}, a sole proprietorship in Cairo, Egypt (commercial register no. {registration}), owned by Dr Khaled Hassanein, who is the data controller: the person who decides why and how information is used. Questions about privacy, or to use your rights: {email}.

points.heading: What the app stores, on your phone
points.body: When you use the app you may enter: your birth year, your language, your period and cycle dates and flow, symptoms, mood, discharge, sexual activity, basal body temperature, ovulation test results, notes you type, weight, appointments, pregnancy and baby-movement logs, contraction timer sessions, and your health record: visits, lab results, scans, medicines with the doses you mark and their reminders, conditions, allergies, procedures, and documents and photos you add. This is health information. Your birth year checks that you are 18 or over, and your age shapes some guidance, such as when the app suggests talking to a clinician while you try to conceive, which tips you see and the questions on your visit summary. All of it is kept in a private file that only the femio app can open, encrypted with a key held by your phone’s secure hardware (the Android Keystore); documents and photos are sealed with the same key, each in its own file. You can also turn on an app lock with a PIN. femio sends nothing from this file to us or to anyone else; the only exceptions are files you choose to share or export, and Cloud boost if you agree to it (both below).

points.heading: What the app never does
points.body: No account, no sign-in, no name, email or phone number. The app does not read your contacts, your location, or the photos and files on your phone: it sees only a photo or file you choose to add, and it does not ask for permission to use your camera, because Android’s own camera app takes the photo. If you tap the microphone, the app asks once for permission to use it: your phone’s own speech recognition turns your voice into text on the phone, and the app never records, keeps or sends your voice. No ads and no advertising ID. No analytics or crash-report tool of its own, no tracking pixel and no data broker. We do not sell or share your information for advertising, and we never use health information for advertising.

points.heading: Everything that can leave your phone
points.body: This is the complete list. Each item happens only in the situation described.

items.lead: Cloud boost, only if you agree.
items.body: On a phone without on-phone AI, and only for the uses you ticked: a general question you approve, with the public source passages it found; or four broad facts about you, shown to you before you agree: your life stage (for example trying to conceive or pregnant), whether your cycles are regular, the kinds of symptom you logged on two or more days in the last month, and how long you have been logging. In a question, numbers, e-mail addresses and links are removed, and you see and edit the exact text before anything is sent. femio does not remove names or other words, so take out anything you do not want to send. A question about yourself, for example one that says “I” or “my”, stays on the phone. The details are in the next section.

items.lead: A genuineness check, with each Cloud boost request.
items.body: Google Play checks that the request comes from the real femio app on a real phone (Firebase App Check with Play Integrity), so nobody can use femio’s AI service from a copied key. Google’s software also adds the names and versions of its own libraries to the request. Like any internet connection, the request shows your phone’s internet address to Google.

If your phone supports Gemini Nano and you tap Download, Android’s AI system service (AICore, run by Google) downloads the model and keeps it up to date, under Google’s terms. Whenever the app uses Google’s AI software, even with Cloud boost off, that software may send Google technical usage data. Google says this can include device and app details, identifiers for this installation, how long a request took, the size of what went in and out, and error codes. femio does not add your records to it.

You install femio from Google Play, which tells us totals such as installs and crashes, under Google’s own policy. If you buy femio Plus, Google Play handles the payment; femio learns only whether you have Plus. Google Play also checks for femio updates, and now and then may show Google’s own box asking you to rate the app; femio sends nothing of yours with either.
When you tap a source or a help link, it opens in your browser, and that website’s own policy applies.

items.lead: Files you share or export, only when you choose.
items.body: When you share a document or your visit summary, Android’s share sheet hands a plain, unencrypted copy to the app you pick; if you copy the summary instead, it goes to your phone’s clipboard. When you save a spreadsheet (CSV) of your logs, it is a plain, unencrypted file, saved where you choose, which can be a cloud drive. femio itself sends none of them; after that, the copy is in your hands, and the app or service you chose applies its own policy.

items.lead: Why, and on what legal basis.
items.body: To summarise trusted sources for your question, and to put your tips in order, on phones that cannot do it on the phone. Because the four facts and your questions are about your health, we use them only with your explicit consent, given separately for each use on the Cloud boost screen.

Google processes it for us through Firebase AI Logic (the Gemini Developer API, on the paid tier), under Google’s data processing terms. Google may process it in the United States or other countries where it has servers. Google relies on the EU–US Data Privacy Framework and standard contractual clauses for these transfers.

femio has no server and keeps none of it. Under the paid terms we use, Google does not use it to improve its products. Google keeps it for up to 55 days to detect misuse, and people at Google may review content that its systems flag as misuse. We keep Google’s optional request logging switched off.

The app keeps a dated record of what you agreed to, and to which version of the consent screen, inside your encrypted file on your phone; femio has no copy. You can see it on the Cloud boost screen, and it goes into your backup file with the rest of your records. A restored backup keeps the record but does not carry the agreement: each phone asks again.

One tap, on the Cloud boost screen or in Settings, Assistant. That stops anything new being sent. Nothing sent carries your name or an account, so neither we nor Google can find your past requests to delete them; Google deletes them within 55 days.

points.heading: Backups are files you save yourself
points.body: femio can save a backup file when you ask. It is encrypted with a passphrase you choose; without that passphrase nobody, including us, can open it or recover it. You choose where it goes: your phone’s files, a cloud drive, an email. After that the file is in your hands, not ours. We have switched off Android’s automatic cloud backup and phone-to-phone transfer for femio, so Google does not copy your records. If you lose or reset your phone and have no backup file, your records are gone. We cannot recover them.

points.heading: Reminders, notifications and the widget
points.body: Reminders are created on your phone; no server sends them. A notification shows only “femio” and “Open the app”, unless you write your own words for a medicine reminder: those words appear on the notification, including on your lock screen. The home-screen widget shows only “femio” and “Open femio” until you turn on details in Settings; then it shows your pregnancy week or your next-period range. To display them, the reminder words and the widget lines are kept on your phone outside your encrypted file, so they are not encrypted there. Keep reminder words vague if other people see your phone.

items.body: Our host (Vercel) keeps ordinary server logs: your internet address, the time, the page you asked for, your browser type and the website you came from. We use them only to keep the site running and safe (our legitimate interest in security). We do not use them for advertising or combine them with anything else. Vercel keeps them for a short period and may process them outside your country under standard contractual clauses.

We count visits with Vercel Web Analytics. It sets no cookie and stores no internet address. It records the page address without anything after it, the website you came from, your country, and your device, system and browser type. Visits are grouped using a code that is deleted after 24 hours, so a visitor cannot be followed from one day to the next. We use the totals to improve the site. We do not use Google Analytics, a Meta pixel or any other tracking tool.

items.lead: Ads on article and topic pages, only if you allow them.
items.body: Some article pages, condition pages and the guide index may show ads from Google AdSense. Google’s consent message asks you first; until you allow ads, no ad is shown and no ad cookie is set, although your browser still loads Google’s ad script and so shows Google your internet address. If you allow ads, Google acts as a separate controller under its own policy. We ask Google to block ads in sensitive categories, and we never place ads on the calculators, the help page or these legal pages. You can change your choice at any time from the privacy settings link Google shows on the page.

items.lead: Your browser’s memory, and one cookie.
items.body: The site sets one cookie, NEXT_LOCALE. It holds only the language of the pages you are reading (for example “en”), so the site keeps you in your language. It is a session cookie: your browser deletes it when you close it. The site may also remember your light or dark choice in your browser’s storage. Neither is used to track you.

items.lead: Calculators and search run in your browser.
items.body: What you type into a calculator is not sent to us or to anyone else.
Some pages link to other sites, such as medical sources and Find A Helpline. Their own policies apply. Our links send the other site only our address, never the page you were reading.

points.heading: Health information and US state laws
points.body: Your cycle, pregnancy and symptom records are health information under laws such as the EU and UK GDPR, Saudi Arabia’s PDPL, Egypt’s Law 151 of 2020 and US state consumer health data laws. Our consumer health data policy, linked at the foot of every page, sets out what Washington’s My Health My Data Act and similar laws ask us to say. In short: we collect health information only on your phone, we share it with no one, and only Cloud boost, with your consent, sends it to Google as our processor.

points.heading: If you need urgent help
points.body: femio is not an emergency service. See the “Need help now?” link in the app and on the site.

points.heading: Age
points.body: femio’s tracker and Cloud boost are for women aged 18 and over. The app asks your birth year; if the year alone cannot tell, one yes or no question asks whether your 18th birthday has passed, and that answer is not saved. If you are under 18, the tracker does not open, and every guide on the website stays open to you. We do not knowingly collect information from anyone under 18.

points.heading: Your rights, and how to use them
points.body: Depending on where you live, you may have the right to see, correct, delete, restrict or move your information, to object, and to withdraw consent at any time without affecting what happened before. Because your records are only on your phone, you hold them: in the app you can look at them, change them, save an encrypted copy and delete everything (Settings, “Delete everything on this phone”). Turn Cloud boost off on its screen. For the website’s server logs, or anything else, write to {email} and we will answer within 30 days. You may also complain to your data protection authority, for example the Personal Data Protection Centre (Egypt), SDAIA (Saudi Arabia), the ICO (United Kingdom), the authority in your EU country, or your state attorney general in the United States.

points.heading: If something goes wrong
points.body: If information we are responsible for is ever exposed, we will tell the authorities and the people affected within the time the law sets, for example 72 hours for the authority in Egypt, Saudi Arabia, the EU and the UK.

points.heading: If this changes
points.body: If we change what leaves your phone or who receives it, we will update this page first and tell you in the app. A change to Cloud boost asks for your consent again before anything new is sent. Earlier versions stay available on request.

points.heading: Where it comes from

points.heading: Who receives it
points.body: Cloud boost: Google LLC, through Firebase AI Logic (Gemini Developer API, paid tier), as our processor, only after your consent and only for the uses you ticked. Google’s privacy contact: policies.google.com/privacy. We have no affiliates that receive it. We do not sell it, and we do not share it with advertisers, data brokers or analytics companies. points.heading: Your consent

points.heading: Your rights
points.body: You can confirm whether we collect or share your consumer health data, see it, get the list of everyone who received it and how to contact them, withdraw consent, and have it deleted. Your records are on your phone, so you can see, export and delete them in the app (Settings, “Delete everything on this phone”). For anything else, write to {email}. We answer within 45 days (once extended by up to 45 more if needed, and we tell you why), free of charge up to twice a year. If we refuse, you can appeal by replying to our answer; we reply in writing within 45 days, and if we still refuse we tell you how to complain to the Washington State Attorney General.

points.heading: Location

terms.title: Terms of use
terms.intro: What femio is and is not, and the rules for using the app and the website.

points.heading: What femio is
points.body: femio gives you information and tools to record and understand your own health: a cycle and pregnancy tracker and a library of guides and calculators. It is for wellness, education and tracking.

points.heading: What femio is not
points.body: It is not medical advice. It is not a medical device. It does not identify a medical condition, choose or change any medicine or care plan, or replace your doctor, midwife or pharmacist. Using femio does not create a doctor and patient relationship.

points.heading: Not a way to avoid pregnancy
points.body: Fertile-window and cycle predictions are estimates. They do not stop a pregnancy from happening and must not be relied on to avoid one. If you do not want to become pregnant, speak to a clinician about a method that is meant for that.

points.heading: Estimates, with ranges
points.body: Predictions are shown as ranges because bodies vary and your entries may be incomplete. A prediction can be wrong. Changes in the timing of your period can have many causes; talk to a clinician if you are worried.

points.heading: Emergencies
points.body: If you may be in danger or have urgent symptoms, call your local emergency number or go to the nearest emergency department. femio cannot call anyone for you and does not watch your entries.

points.heading: Who may use the app
points.body: You must be 18 or older to use the tracker. The guides on the website are open to everyone.

points.heading: Your responsibilities
points.body: Enter information truthfully for your own use. Keep your phone secure. Keep your backup files private. Do not copy, resell or take apart the app or the site, overload the site, or use either to harm anyone.

points.heading: Your records are yours, and on your phone
points.body: We do not hold them, so we cannot restore them, move them or recover them. Save a backup if you want a copy.

points.heading: What we own
points.body: The femio name, logo, software, design and original guides belong to {entity}. Guidance we cite from medical bodies belongs to them and is credited. You may read and use femio for yourself; you may not copy our content for commercial use without written permission.

points.heading: Limits
points.body: femio is provided as it is. We work hard to be accurate and we cite our sources, but no tool can know your situation, and decisions about your health are for you and your clinician. To the extent the law allows, {entity} is not liable for loss caused by relying on femio instead of professional care. Nothing in these terms limits liability that the law does not allow to be limited, such as fraud or gross fault, or removes rights you have as a consumer.

points.heading: Changes and ending
points.body: We may update these terms and the app. If a change matters to you we will say so in the app. You can stop using femio at any time by deleting everything and removing the app.

points.heading: Law
points.body: These terms are governed by the laws of the Arab Republic of Egypt, and the competent courts of Cairo decide disputes, except that mandatory consumer rules of the country where you live still apply to you, including in Saudi Arabia, and nothing here stops you from using rights or courts that those rules give you.

pmb.heading: Bleeding after twelve months? Get it checked

Coming to Google Play.
getApp.bodyLive: A private Android app for trying to conceive and pregnancy, with an assistant that runs on your phone. Your calendar, logs and pregnancy tools stay on your phone, behind a PIN if you choose. No account, and nothing from your records goes to the cloud unless you turn on Cloud boost.

today.title: Today, at a glance
today.body: Your fertile window and next period as ranges with a confidence word, when to test, and your temperatures.

calendar.title: The next three periods
calendar.body: Each later period is a wider range, with “no confident window” when your cycles vary too much.

ask.title: Ask femio
ask.body: Health answers only from trusted sources carried on your phone, each sentence numbered to its source.

sayIt.title: Say it to log
sayIt.body: Write how you feel in your own words, and femio turns it into log entries you confirm.

tips.title: Tips for you
tips.body: Reviewed sentences with their source, chosen on your phone from what you log.

visit.title: Visit summary
visit.body: A page for your doctor: your cycles, what you logged most, and questions you could ask.

pregnancy.title: Pregnancy tools
pregnancy.body: Your week and due date, a movement log, a contraction timer and a weight log.

private.title: Private by design
private.body: Your records are kept on your phone, not on our servers. Add a PIN lock, and save a backup file yourself.

languages.title: Four languages
languages.body: English, Arabic, French and Spanish, with right-to-left layout built in for Arabic.

doctor.title: Appointments
doctor.body: Keep your appointments and the questions you want to ask in one place.

getApp.meanwhileBody: Everything on this website is free and needs no account.
getApp.notMedical: femio is for tracking and learning, not medical advice, and its estimates are not a way to avoid pregnancy. Talk to your clinician about your health.
getApp.companion: The assistant is a companion, not the engine: every feature works with it switched off, and it never adds anything to your log without you.

testBuild.title: Early test build (APK)
testBuild.body: For people testing or reviewing femio: an Android build you install yourself, before femio is on Google Play. Google Play closed testing comes later.
testBuild.soonBody: The test build will be linked here once it is published. Until then, everything on this website is free to use.

steps.download: On your Android phone, tap “Download the APK”.
steps.allow: If Android asks, allow installs from this source: your browser or your Files app.
steps.open: Open the downloaded APK and tap Install. You can switch that permission off again afterwards.

tour.heading: femio, screen by screen.
tour.sub: Real screens from the app, filled with sample data. Pick a screen, or let them play.
tour.languagesNote: The app is in English, Arabic, French and Spanish.
tour.synthetic: Sample data, not a real person's.

today.label: Today
today.title: Today, as a dashboard
today.body: Your fertile window and next period as ranges with a confidence word, when to test, your temperatures, and tips chosen on your phone. Notices come last.
today.alt: The femio Today screen: a fertile-window range, a when-to-test card, buttons to log, and three tips with their sources.

calendar.label: Calendar
calendar.title: The next three periods
calendar.body: Each later period is a wider range, and a low-confidence one is drawn dashed. When your cycles vary, only the next one is shown.
calendar.alt: The femio calendar with predicted days in outline and a card listing the next three periods, each with a confidence word.

ask.label: Ask femio
ask.title: Answers that show their sources
ask.body: femio answers only from health sources it carries on your phone and numbers each one. When they do not cover a question, it says so instead of guessing.
ask.alt: Ask femio answering a question about period cramps, with numbered MedlinePlus sources.

boost.label: Cloud boost
boost.title: Cloud boost stays off unless you agree
boost.body: For phones without on-phone AI. You agree to each use separately, and you see exactly what would be sent before anything is.
boost.alt: The AI and Cloud boost screen: the statements she ticks and a separate consent box for each use, before she confirms.

visit.label: Visit summary
visit.title: A page for your doctor
visit.body: Made from what you logged, with questions you could ask. It stays on your phone unless you copy it.
visit.alt: The visit summary: cycles logged, what was logged most in 90 days, and questions to ask.

periods.heading: Honest about how far ahead it can see.
periods.body: Pick a pattern. This works out the next periods with the same rule the app uses.

notes.regular: Four periods logged, 28 or 29 days apart.
notes.varies: Four periods logged, between 24 and 35 days apart.
notes.new: One period logged, and a usual cycle of 28 days.

periods.caption: Sample dates. Nothing you tap here is saved or sent.

sayIt.heading: Say it, and it becomes your log.
sayIt.body: Write how you feel in your own words. femio turns it into the same chips you would tap, and you untick anything that is wrong.

samples.cramps: Bad cramps and a headache today, so tired
samples.bloated: Feeling bloated and nauseous this morning
samples.back: Back pain and I feel anxious

sayIt.demoNote: A demo with sample sentences. It runs in your browser and saves nothing.

ask.heading: Ask femio, and see where every sentence comes from.

questions.bleeding: Heavy bleeding and I feel dizzy
questions.uncovered: What is the capital of France?

ask.crampsAnswer: Heat on your lower belly and some exercise may ease period pain [1]. Contact a doctor if self-care does not help and the pain gets in the way of your life [2].
ask.rulesFirst: Safety rules run before any AI. Here femio did not ask the AI at all: signs of danger open help first.
ask.demoNote: A demo with a sample answer. In the app, Gemini Nano writes it on your phone from the passages femio carries.

privacy.heading: Your records stay on your phone. Here is everything else.
privacy.body: The app has no ads, no analytics of its own and no tracking tools. This is the complete list of what can ever leave your phone, and when.

cloud.title: Cloud boost, only if you agree
cloud.body: On a phone without on-phone AI, and only for the uses you ticked: a general question you approve, sent with the public sources it found, after numbers, e-mail addresses and links are removed and you have seen and edited the exact text; or four broad facts shown to you first: your life stage, whether your cycles are regular, the kinds of symptom you logged, and how long you have been logging.

check.title: A genuineness check, with each Cloud boost request
check.body: Google Play confirms the request comes from the real femio app on a real phone. Like any internet connection, the request shows your phone's internet address to Google.

model.title: Google's on-phone AI
model.body: Whenever the app uses Google's AI software, even with Cloud boost off, it may send Google technical usage data, such as device details, an identifier for this installation, errors and performance. If you tap Download, Android's AI service (AICore, run by Google) downloads Gemini Nano and keeps it up to date. femio adds none of your records to it.

play.title: Google Play
play.body: You install femio from Google Play, which tells us totals such as installs and crashes. If you buy femio Plus, Google Play handles the payment.

links.title: Links you open
links.body: A source or help link opens in your browser, under that website's own policy.

share.title: Files you share or export
share.body: A document, your visit summary or a spreadsheet of your logs goes as a plain, unencrypted copy, only to the app or place you pick.

backup.title: Backups you save yourself
backup.body: A backup file is encrypted with a passphrase you choose, and goes only where you put it.

app.predictionNote: Predictions are estimates, not guarantees, and must not be relied on to avoid pregnancy.
app.upcomingPeriodsWider: Each later period is a wider range: the further ahead, the less certain.
app.upcomingPeriodsOnlyNext: Only the next period is shown: your logged cycles vary too much, or there are too few yet, to reach further ahead.
app.askIntro: Ask a health question. femio answers only from trusted health sources it carries on your phone, such as CDC, MedlinePlus and the Office on Women's Health, and shows where every sentence came from.
app.askAnswerOnPhone: Summarised on your phone by Gemini Nano, from the sources below
app.askClinicianLine: This is general information, not advice for you. For your own situation, talk to your clinician.
app.askNotCovered: femio's trusted sources don't answer this, so femio won't guess. Try other words, read the links below, or ask your clinician.
app.safetyHeavyBleedingBody: ACOG says: “If you are changing pads or tampons every hour for more than 2 hours in a row, and you also have chest pain, have shortness of breath, and are lightheaded or dizzy, seek emergency medical care right away.” If that is you, call your local emergency number now. If heavy bleeding worries you, talk to your doctor.
app.sayItFound: femio found these. Untick anything that is wrong.
app.sayItSaveCount: Save {entries, plural, one{1 entry} other{{entries} entries}} on {days, plural, one{1 day} other{{days} days}}
app.assistantPrivateNote: This runs on your phone. femio does not send your words anywhere.
app.tipsChosenOnPhone: Chosen on your phone from your log. Each tip is a reviewed sentence with its source.
app.tip_folicAcidBeforePregnancy: Folic acid, a B vitamin, is advised from at least a month before pregnancy. Ask a clinician how to get enough.
app.tip_regularSexTakesTime: Most couples where the woman is under 40 conceive within a year of regular sex every 2 to 3 days. It can take time.
app.tip_testingTooEarly: Testing very early can give a false negative. Follow the test's own instructions.
app.visitIntro: A page to show your clinician, made from what you logged. It stays on your phone unless you share or copy it.
app.boostIntro: Some phones have no on-phone AI. On those phones, Cloud boost lets Google's cloud AI summarise trusted sources for a question you approve, or put your tips in order. It is optional and stays off unless you agree below. Everything else in femio works without it.
app.boostCategoriesLabel: Kinds of symptom logged in the last month
app.boostNever: Nothing else from your record: not your log, notes, dates, cycle lengths, medicines, lab results, visits, documents, photos or birth year. Never your contacts or advertising ID.
app.boostAlsoSeen: Like any internet connection, Google also sees your phone's internet address, and a check from Google Play that the request comes from the real femio app.
app.boostWithdrawEffect: Turning it off stops anything new being sent. It cannot recall what was already sent.

pcosChecklist.metaDescription: A printable PCOS list to bring to your clinician: things you have noticed and questions to ask, from femio's cited guides. It is not a test.
pcosChecklist.title: PCOS visit checklist
pcosChecklist.intro: A list to bring to your clinician; it is not a test.
pcosChecklist.note: Other health issues can cause similar changes, so a symptom list cannot confirm PCOS.
pcosChecklist.privacy: femio does not save or send your ticks. They are only for your printout.
pcosChecklist.experiencesHint: Tick what applies to you. You can also tick on paper.
pcosChecklist.rapid: Rapid new hair growth, a deepening voice, or other fast body changes need prompt medical assessment because they are less typical of PCOS.
pcosChecklist.urgentBody: Get urgent medical help for very heavy bleeding with fainting, severe weakness, chest pain, or trouble breathing. Sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain also needs prompt assessment. Contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department.
pcosChecklist.urgentMood: If you have thoughts of ending your life or of harming yourself, get help now. Visit the <help>help page</help> for support routes. You can also contact local emergency services or go to the nearest emergency department.
pcosChecklist.guidesTitle: femio guides this list comes from
pcosChecklist.hubBody: Print a list of things you have noticed and questions to ask your clinician. It is not a test.

experiences.periodsStop: Periods that stop for several months
experiences.hardToPredict: Bleeding that is hard to predict
experiences.heavyAfterGap: Heavy bleeding after a long gap
experiences.coarseHair: Coarse hair growth on the face, chest, abdomen, or back
experiences.acne: Acne that continues beyond the teenage years or is hard to manage
experiences.darkPatches: Changes linked with insulin resistance, such as darker, thicker patches of skin
experiences.ovulationTiming: Difficulty knowing whether or when ovulation occurs
experiences.lowMood: Low mood or worry lasts, or keeps coming back
experiences.eatingBodyImage: Worries about eating or body image
experiences.snoring: Snoring, together with waking up unrefreshed, feeling sleepy in the day, or tiredness

questions.criteria: Which criteria apply in my case?
questions.otherCauses: What other causes are you checking?
questions.medicines: How could my medicines affect the results?
questions.longTerm: Which long-term health checks are relevant to me?
questions.reviewFindings: When will we review the findings?
questions.acneOtherCause: Could my acne or hair change have another cause we should check?
questions.moodCheck: Would a mood check fit this visit?
questions.support: What support is available near me, such as talking therapy?
questions.hairSkinOption: Which hair or skin option fits my goals?
questions.sugarTest: Do I need a sugar drink test (OGTT) or another blood test?
questions.heartRisk: Should I have a check for heart and blood vessel risk?
questions.repeatSugar: When should we repeat my blood sugar checks?
questions.goalFirst: Which goal should we focus on first?
questions.optionWhy: Which option fits that goal, and why?
questions.notTrying: Which options would you suggest if I am not trying to get pregnant?
questions.sideEffects: What side effects should I watch for with each option?
questions.habits: Which healthy habits would help my goals most, such as periods, fertility or blood sugar?
questions.sleepCheck: Should I have a sleep check if I snore and feel tired during the day?
questions.weightTalk: Can we talk about weight only when I say yes?
